content: Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), also known as chronic otitis media (COM), is a persistent inflammatory condition of the middle ear and mastoid cavity. It is often caused by polymicrobial infections, meaning it involves more than one type of microorganism. The condition is characterized by ear discharge (otorrhoea) through a perforated tympanic membrane, and its primary symptoms include ear discharge and hearing loss. Topical antibiotics are the most commonly used treatment for CSOM. These medications work by either killing or inhibiting the growth of the microorganisms responsible for the infection. They can be used as a standalone treatment or in combination with other interventions, such as antiseptics or ear cleaning procedures (aural toileting). The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of topical antibiotics (without steroids) in individuals with CSOM. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, to identify relevant published and unpublished trials. The search was completed on April 1, 2019. The study included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with a minimum follow-up period of one week. Participants included both adults and children with chronic ear discharge of unknown cause or CSOM, where the discharge had persisted for more than two weeks. The interventions studied involved the application of topical antibiotics directly into the ear canal in various forms, such as ear drops, powders, or irrigations, either alone or as part of an aural toileting procedure. The main comparisons were between topical antibiotics and placebo or no treatment, as well as between different types of topical antibiotics. The researchers used standard Cochrane methodological procedures and the GRADE system to assess the certainty of the evidence for each outcome. The primary outcomes of interest were the resolution of ear discharge (or achieving a dry ear), health-related quality of life, and ear pain or discomfort. Secondary outcomes included hearing, serious complications, and ototoxicity. Seventeen studies involving a total of 2,198 participants were included in the analysis. Twelve studies reported participant numbers, totaling 1,797 individuals, while five studies reported both participant and ear numbers, representing 401 participants and 510 ears. Comparison A: Topical antibiotics versus placebo or no treatment (with aural toileting in both groups and no other background treatment) One small study compared ciprofloxacin ear drops to a placebo (saline). All participants underwent aural toileting. Ciprofloxacin was more effective than saline in resolving ear discharge at one to two weeks, with 84% of participants achieving resolution compared to 12% in the placebo group (risk ratio [RR] 6.74, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.82 to 24.99; 35 participants). However, the certainty of this evidence was very low, making it unclear whether ciprofloxacin is definitively better. The study reported no medical side effects or worsening of hearing related to the topical medication. Comparison B: Topical antibiotics versus placebo or no treatment (with systemic antibiotics in both groups) Four studies compared topical ciprofloxacin to no topical treatment (three studies, 190 participants) or topical ceftizoxime to no topical treatment (one study, 248 participants). In all studies, participants received the same systemic antibiotic (oral ciprofloxacin or injected ceftizoxime). At least one study included aural toileting for all participants. Data from three studies showed that ciprofloxacin was more effective than no treatment, with 88.2% of participants achieving resolution of discharge at one to two weeks compared to 60% in the no-treatment group (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.20 to 1.80; 2 studies, 150 participants). The certainty of this evidence was low. None of the studies reported on ear pain, discomfort, or local irritation. Comparison C: Different types of topical antibiotics The evidence comparing different topical antibiotics was of very low certainty. Quinolones versus aminoglycosides: Seven studies compared aminoglycosides (gentamicin, neomycin, or tobramycin) to quinolones (ciprofloxacin or ofloxacin) in 734 and 214 participants, respectively. Quinolones appeared to result in higher rates of discharge resolution at one to two weeks, but the very low certainty of the evidence makes it unclear whether quinolones are superior (RR 1.95, 95% CI 0.88 to 4.29; 6 studies, 694 participants). One study reported no difference in ear pain between the groups. Quinolones versus aminoglycosides/polymyxin B combinations (± gramicidin): Three studies were identified, but only one provided data on the primary outcome. Ciprofloxacin was compared to a neomycin/polymyxin B/gramicidin combination for an unknown treatment duration (likely four weeks). Ciprofloxacin was more effective (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.22; 186 participants). A few patients experienced local irritation during the first application of the topical treatment, but the specific numbers and groups were not reported. Other comparisons: Limited data were available for other comparisons, such as gentamicin versus a trimethoprim/sulphacetamide/polymyxin B combination (91 participants) and rifampicin versus chloramphenicol (160 participants). The findings were highly uncertain. Conclusions: The effectiveness of topical antibiotics in resolving ear discharge in patients with CSOM remains uncertain due to the limited amount of low-quality evidence available. However, there is some evidence suggesting that topical antibiotics may be effective when compared to placebo or when used alongside systemic antibiotics. The relative effectiveness of different types of topical antibiotics, such as quinolones versus aminoglycosides, is also uncertain. These two classes of antibiotics have different adverse effect profiles, but the included studies provided insufficient data to draw conclusions about these effects. Overall, adverse effects were poorly reported across the studies.
